core.text: When something is *so* big, *so* fast, *so* foolish *that* something follows, Latin uses **ut + subjunctive after tam / ita / tantus (the 'so … that' clause)**. A signal word — *tam* (so, before an adjective or adverb), *ita* or *sīc* (in such a way), *tantus* (so big), *tālis* (of such a kind), *tot* (so many) — is answered by *ut* and a verb in the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do). Latin name: *coniūnctīvus cōnsecūtīvus*.
English: she was *so* tired *that* she fell asleep. The *so … that* pair is the whole idea; Latin only adds a special verb form in the *that* part.
Signal word (tam, ita, sīc, tantus, tālis, tot) + ut + subjunctive = result. The negative is ut nōn, not nē.

invented.la: Puer tam fessus erat ut statim dormīret.
invented.en: The boy was so tired that he fell asleep at once.

invented.la: Tanta erat tempestās ut nāvis nōn movērētur.
invented.en: The storm was so great that the ship did not move.

core.text: Purpose also uses *ut*, but has no signal word and its negative is *nē*. Test: can you add 'in order'? *vēnit ut vidēret* = came in order to see (purpose); *tam fessus erat ut dormīret* = so tired that he slept (result). *ut nōn* is always result.

more.text: The learner's notes sort the signal words by what is measured: *tam* for the degree of an adjective (*tam fortis est ut …*), *tantus* for the size of a thing, *tālis* for its kind, *ita* for the manner of an action (*ita clāmat ut audiātur*, he shouts so that he is heard), *tot* for a number. Sometimes the signal word is left out; then only sense decides — a purpose is intended but not necessarily achieved, a result is achieved but not necessarily intended.

The tense follows the sequence of tenses: *ita clāmō ut proximōs suscitem* (I shout so as to wake the neighbours) but *ita clāmāvī ut … suscitārem*. Ørberg's chapter 29: *Dāvus ita clāmat ut puerum excitet*; *Syra tam quiēta erat ut puellam nōn excitāret*.

Also easy to confuse: an indirect command, *ut* after a verb of ordering or asking (*imperat ut taceat*, orders him to be quiet) — no signal word, negative *nē*. And verbs meaning 'bring it about' take a result-style clause: *faciam* — I will see to it — *ut tergum eī doleat*, that his back hurts (Week 4).
In a result sentence the first half measures; the *ut* half reports what came of it. Nobody intended anything: this is an outcome, not an aim.
Meet one of the signal words (*tam, tantus, tālis, ita, sīc*) and expect an *ut* clause further on to answer it.

teach.title: So far that something follows

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence tells you what followed from the 'so'?

teach.say: When something is *so* far along that something comes of it, Latin pairs a signal word with **ut + subjunctive after tam / ita / tantus (the 'so … that' clause)**. *Puer tam fessus est ut statim dormiat* — the boy is so tired that he falls asleep at once.

teach.title: The signal words
teach.say: Learn the words that call for this *ut*: **tam** (so, in front of an adjective or an adverb), **tantus -a -um** (so great), **tālis** (of such a kind), **ita** and **sīc** (in such a way). *Tantus est clāmor ut nēmō audiat* — the shouting is so loud that nobody hears.

check.ask: Ita has already told you what to expect: what is the ut clause after it?

teach.title: The negative is ut nōn
teach.say: Because the *ut* half reports what actually happened, its negative is **ut nōn** — never *nē*. *Tanta est tempestās ut nāvis nōn moveātur*: the storm is so great that the ship is not moved. Seeing *ut nōn* is enough on its own to tell you the clause is a result, because an aim would have had *nē*.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of possum that ut … nōn needs here.

teach.title: Result, not purpose
teach.say: Purpose and result share the word *ut*, so use two tests. First: is there a signal word (*tam, ita, tantus, tālis*)? Only result has one. Second: can you put 'in order' in front of the English? *runs so fast that nobody sees him* — nobody is trying to be unseen, so it is result.

check.ask: What is rīdeant here — the aim, or what came of it?

teach.title: The same pattern in a past story
teach.say: Nothing about the pattern changes when the story is in the past; only the tense of the subjunctive does. *Tantus erat timor ut omnēs fugerent* — the fear was so great that everybody fled: the past *erat* calls for the imperfect subjunctive (the past-time 'might / would' form: venīret; built on the infinitive) *fugerent* in place of *fugiant*.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of fugiō that the past main verb calls for.
